Civil Rights Era. Roughly nineteen fifty to nineteen seventy, with earlier and later contexts. The period of intense literary and cultural production by African American and allied writers exploring, protesting, and reimagining racial justice, identity, and Black humanity in the United States. African American literature became increasingly central to American letters, with writers like Maya Angelou, Lorraine Hansberry, and Alice Walker achieving unprecedented visibility and creating canonical works.

The Civil Rights Era emerged from earlier African American literary traditions including the Harlem Renaissance and Blues and Jazz poetry, but intensified dramatically after World War II as legal segregation and de facto racism intensified political mobilization. Maya Angelou's autobiographical work I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings established Black women's autobiographical testimony as a powerful literary form for exploring trauma, resilience, and the political dimensions of personal narrative.

Lorraine Hansberry brought Black family drama to Broadway with A Raisin in the Sun, centering working-class Black aspiration and dignity on stages where Black lives had previously been spectacle or absent. Alice Walker revived the legacy of Zora Neale Hurston and created narratives of Black women's resilience and sexuality—particularly in The Color Purple—that challenged both racism and sexism simultaneously.

Civil Rights Era writers wrote across genres—poetry, drama, essay, autobiography, fiction—creating a multimedia artistic response to social crisis. The era saw increasing Black literary self-determination with Black publishing houses, Black-edited journals, and Black-curated literary circles emerging as alternatives to mainstream institutional gatekeeping. Writers navigated complicated relationships to protest and art, but nearly all saw their work as intervening in political struggle, making the Civil Rights Era a moment when literature became a vital instrument of activism and social transformation.
